19  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
20       Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction, possessing only those powers granted by 
21  the Constitution and by statute. See United States v. Marks, 530 F.3d 799, 810 (9th Cir. 2008). 

22  “It is to be presumed that a cause lies outside this limited jurisdiction, and the burden of 
23  establishing the contrary rests upon the party asserting jurisdiction.” Id. (internal citations 
24  omitted).  “The ‘strong presumption against removal jurisdiction means that the defendant has 
25  the burden of establishing that removal is proper,’ and the court resolves all ambiguity in favor 
1  of remand to state court.” Hunter v. Philip Morris USA, 582 F.3d 1039, 1042 (9th Cir. 2009) 
2  (quoting Gaus v. Miles, Inc., 980 F.2d 564, 566 (9th Cir. 1992) (per curiam)). 
3       Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a) provides for removal of a civil action from state to 
4  federal court if the case could have originated in federal court.  Under 28 U.S.C. § 1331, a 
5  federal district court has jurisdiction over cases “arising under the Constitution, laws, or treaties 
6  of the United States.”  “The presence or absence of federal-question jurisdiction is governed by 
7  the ‘well-pleaded complaint rule,’ which provides that federal jurisdiction exists only when a 
8  federal question is presented on the face of the plaintiff’s properly pleaded complaint.” 
9  Caterpillar Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386, 388 (1987).                   
10       “[A] case can ‘aris[e] under’ federal law in two ways.  Most directly, a case arises under 
11  federal law when federal law creates the cause of action asserted.” Gunn v. Minton, 568 U.S. 
12  251, 257 (2013).  Alternatively, “when ‘a claim finds its origins’ in state law, there is ‘a special 
13  and small category of cases in which arising under jurisdiction still lies.’” Merrill Lynch, 
14  Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. v. Manning, 578 U.S. 374, 383 (2016) (quoting Gunn v. Minton, 
15  568 U.S. 251, 258 (2013)).  In Grable, the Supreme Court stated that “federal jurisdiction over 
16  a state law claim will lie if a federal issue is: (1) necessarily raised, (2) actually disputed, (3) 
17  substantial, and (4) capable of resolution in federal court without disrupting the federal-state 
18  balance approved by Congress.” Gunn, 568 U.S. at 528 (citing Grable & Sons Metal Prods., 
19  Inc. v. Darue Eng’g & Mfg., 545 U.S. 308, 313–14 (2005)).

1  III.  DISCUSSION                                                          
2       Plaintiff brings three causes of action, all under Nevada state law.  Thus, the question is 
3  whether Plaintiff’s Complaint, specifically his references to federal law and regulations in 
4   pleading Defendants’ alleged conduct, nevertheless confers this Court with federal jurisdiction 
5  under the Grable doctrine.3  For the reasons set forth below, the Court finds that it does not.    
6       Beginning with the first factor, Plaintiff argues that a federal issue is not “necessarily  
7  raised” because his claims are predicated on Nevada state law, and only reference violations of 
8  federal law as an alternative basis for his state law claims. (Mot. Remand 8:4–9:25, ECF No. 
9  13); (Reply 8:23–9:18, ECF No. 42).  In response, Defendants maintain that a federal issue is 
10  necessarily raised because Plaintiff’s Complaint expressly invokes federal law and the 
11  determination of Plaintiff’s claims require interpretation of federal law.4 (Resp. 15:10–16:10, 
12  ECF No. 37).                                                              
13       Several courts have considered similar scenarios to the one before this Court, where 
14  allegations for claims such as fraud, breach of fiduciary duty, unjust enrichment, and corporate

8  14, 2007); Fagin v. Gilmartin, No. 03-cv-2631, 2007 WL 419286 (D.N.J. Feb. 1, 2007); 
9  Gargiulo v. Decker, No. 05-cv-00103, 2015 WL 755771 (C.D. Cal. Mar. 30, 2005); In re 
10  Textainer P’Ship Secs. Litig., No. 05-cv-0969, 2005 WL 1791559 (N.D. Cal. July 27, 2005). 
11       Ekas is particularly instructive.  In Ekas, the plaintiffs filed a verified derivative 
12  complaint by shareholders on behalf of a nominal defendant against several members of its 
13  board of directors and executive officers for breach of fiduciary duties and unjust enrichment. 
14  Id. at *1–2.  The plaintiffs argued that there was no federal question to support removal because 
15  their claims arose under state law. Id. The plaintiffs further contended that a complaint alleging 
16  state law claims based in part on false statements in documents required by federal securities 
17  law cannot be removed. Id.  In opposition, the defendants claimed that, to adjudicate fully the 
18  allegations in the complaint, the court would need to resolve multiple questions of federal law. 
19  Id. at *4.  The defendants pointed to various allegations in the complaint that they claimed 
20  showed that the violations of law stemmed from the alleged failure of the defendants to have in 
21  place a federally mandated control structure that ensured the accuracy of financial information 

22  and compliance with GAAP. Id.  Additionally, the defendants asserted that the plaintiffs had 
23  sought to avoid federal question jurisdiction through artful pleading since it was actually 
24  federal law, not state law, that provided the duties and obligations at issue. Id. 
25  ///                                                                       
1       The Ekas court agreed with the plaintiffs and found that the plaintiffs’ “passing 
2  references” to federal law in the complaint were not essential to proving any of the elements of 
3  the state causes of action alleged therein. Id.  The court found that, although the duty to comply 
4  with federal laws was one of many duties that were allegedly breached by the defendants, the 
5  “gravamen” of the breach of fiduciary duty rested upon the defendants “knowingly approving 
6  the Company's violation of GAAP.” Id.  The court explained that, “[c]learly, in proving that a 
7  breach of fiduciary duty occurred, [p]laintiffs may point to evidence that the officers and 
8  directors failed to act in good faith when they made false statements. But the fact that some of 
9  those false statements were made to the SEC and may have violated federal law [was] 
10  tangential to proving the breach of fiduciary duty.” Id. at *4.  The court found that adjudication 
11  of federal law would not be necessary because the complaint contained “[a]llegations that 
12  simply provided a factual basis for a [state law or federal law] claim.” Id. at *5.   
13       Although the defendants in Ekas made much of the fact that the complaint tracked the 
14  language of Section 13 of the Exchange Act, the court found that mere reference to federal 
15  securities law was insufficient and that such allegations were included in the complaint to 
16  simply set forth the various duties of the directors and officers of the defendants. Id.  Thus, if 
17  those allegations were proven, they would provide evidence of the defendants’ role in the 
18  company but would not require an examination of federal law. Id.  In other words, the court 
19  rejected the defendants' contention that it would “need to construe and interpret the Exchange 
20  Act and Sarbanes–Oxley [Act] and whether defendants violated provisions of those federal 
21  laws.”  Instead, the court found that it only needed to examine evidence relating to the 

22  defendants' maintenance of the accounting of the company and, while there might be 
23  similarities to federal accounting requirements, that inquiry would not require the court to delve 
24  into federal law. Ekas, at *5.                                            
25  ///                                                                       
1       Applying Ekas and similar cases to the instant action, although Plaintiff is the “master of 
2  his complaint,” the relevant inquiry is whether he crafted the complaint in such a way that it 
3  relied solely on state law.  For example, if Plaintiff’s Complaint explicitly pled violations of 
4  federal law as the basis for this claims, this action was properly removed to federal court for 
5  disposition, regardless of how the claims are labeled in the Complaint.  However, if violations 
6  of federal securities law are an alternative way of proving the conduct, and instead merely 
7  provide a factual basis for Plaintiff’s state claims, then references alone to federal law are 
8  insufficient to create federal jurisdiction.  Thus, the Court is driven by the substance of the 
9  allegations underlying claim rather than its label.                       
10      Returning to Defendants’ argument, the Court disagrees with Defendants that Plaintiff’s 
11  Complaint necessarily raises issues of federal law. (Resp. 14:10–23).  Throughout the 
12  Complaint, Plaintiff alleges that Defendants violated relevant legal and regulatory 
13  requirements, which include CleanSpark’s own internal policies, state securities laws, and 
14  federal securities laws. (Compl. ¶¶ 34–35,48, 191(c), 203(iii), Ex. A to Pet. Removal).  It is true 
15  that these allegations include general references to federal securities law.  But mere references 
16  to federal law is insufficient to create federal question jurisdiction. Gargiulo, 2005 WL 755771, 
17  at *2–3 (finding state law claim for breach of fiduciary duty raised no federal claim because 
18  “although the complaint discusses possible violations of federal securities law, such references 
19  are not ‘essential elements’ of any of [p]laintiff’s state law claims”); In re Textainer P’Ship 
20  Secs. Litig., 2005 WL 1791559, at *8 (finding state law claim for breach of fiduciary duty 
21  raised no federal claim because such references were not an essential element of any of the 

22  plaintiff’s state law claims); Emulex Corp. v. Broadcom Corp., No. 09-cv-0677, 2009 WL 
23  1872694, at *4 (C.D. Cal. June 29, 2009) (“While Emulex’s fraud claim may embrace a point 
24  of federal securities law, federal law did not create Emulex’s claim and is not essential in 
25  determining whether Emulex has a right to relief.”).                      
1      Here, the gravamen of the misconduct alleged by Plaintiff does not depend on the 
2  interpretation of federal securities law. See Franchise Tax Bd. v. Constr. Laborers Vacation Tr., 
3  463 U.S. 1, 9 (1983) (stating that “[w]e have often held that a case ‘arose under’ federal law 
4  where the vindication of a right under state law necessarily turned on some construction of 
5  federal law”).  Instead, it is premised on whether Defendants violated a special duty of care 
6  governed by state law in the case of the fiduciary duty and corporate waste claims, and whether 
7  they unduly benefited pursuant to the unjust enrichment claim. (See Mot. Remand 8:17–9:25) 
8  (citing the elements of a breach of fiduciary duty, unjust enrichment, and corporate waste 
9  claims under Nevada law).  Indeed, Plaintiff’s Complaint identifies that Defendants conducted 
10  violated CleanSpark’s own Internal Code of Conduct and Governance, state securities law, and 
11  federal securities law.  Thus, “[f]ailure to comply with federal securities law is alleged as one 
12  of the many charged consequences of the Defendants’ mismanagement.  Whether federal 
13  securities laws were in fact violated is not a necessary element of determining whether 
14  Defendants’ alleged mismanagement rose to the level of a breach of fiduciary duty[,]” unjust 
15  enrichment, or corporate waste. Fagin, 2007 WL 419286, at *5.             
16      Defendants additionally argue that federal law is implicated because the allegedly false 
17  or misleading statements were made in SEC filings, press releases, and other public documents. 
18  (Resp. 15:11–17:13).  However, this argument has been routinely rejected by district courts. 
19  See Randolph, 2010 WL 5148293, at *7 (“Likewise, defendant’s failure in this case to comply 
20  with federal rules by misrepresenting or omitting information on federally-required forms 
21  would simply provide some evidence of a breach, but the Court need not construe federal law 

22  in order for plaintiff to recover.”); Ekas, 2007 WL 4055630, at *4 (“Clearly, in proving that a 
23  breach of fiduciary duty occurred, [p]laintiffs may point to evidence that he officers and 
24  directors failed to act in good faith when they made false statements. But the fact that some of 
25  the false statements were made to the SEC and may have violated federal law [was] tangential 
1  to proving the breach of fiduciary duty.”); Fagin, 2007 WL 419286, at *4 (“In the Court’s 
2  opinion, however, these factual predicates alleging that one component of the alleged 
3  wrongdoing was, in essence, making false filings with the SEC, do not transform the state 
4  claims into claims seeking redress for federal violations and do not raise a substantial and 
5  disputed question of federal law.”).  Indeed, “the fact ‘that the [allegedly false] statements were 
6  made in a federally required document does not change the inquiry [into] whether, standing 
7  alone, they were false or misleading . . . under state law.” Flynn ex rel. Moody’s Corp., 689 F. 
8  Supp. 2d at 691 (quoting Sung v. Wasserstein, 415 F. Supp. 2d 393, 406 (S.D.N.Y. 2006); see 
9  Merrell Dow Pharms., Inc. v. Thompson, 478 U.S. 804, 813 (1986) (“The mere presence of a
